title: Responses parity triage: streaming, tool-call, schema reconciliation plan
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: We continue to see production and integration tests highlight behavioral differences between Redwood's Responses API and OpenAI's Responses semantics across three overlapping areas: 1) streaming event sequencing and partial JSON emission, 2) function/tool-calling signal semantics (early calls vs final call), and 3) structured/schemata outputs that are occasionally malformed when streamed. These differences cause SDK consumers to mis-handle tool invocation, drop partially emitted objects, or mis-interpret EOF semantics when assembling structured outputs.

Goal: Produce a prioritized, implementable plan to triage parity gaps, ship runtime adapter mitigations that preserve low latency for streaming use-cases, and create a regression harness plus canary rollout to validate behavior against representative OpenAI Responses samples. This ticket covers analysis, adapter design, prototype, and canary plan for runtime-1.20.

Scope (this ticket):
- Inventory concrete behavioral deltas with examples (event sequences, chunk shapes, sample payloads).
- Design an in-runtime adapter layer that can: 1) reassemble partial JSON objects across stream chunks, 2) detect/normalize function call start/continue/end events to align caller semantics, and 3) apply best-effort schema repair with configurable strict/lenient modes.
- Build a lightweight prototype (hot-path optimized) with metrics hooks.
- Define canary test cases and rollout/rollback criteria.

Out of scope: full API contract change; long-term contract negotiation with OpenAI; large-scale model re-training.

Acceptance criteria:
- Inventory document with at least 25 unique recorded deltas and concrete reproducible inputs/outputs.
- Prototype adapter that passes the regression harness for 90% of recorded streaming cases without adding >5ms median tail latency for 90th percentile request sizes.
- Canary plan and dashboards defined; alerting for parity-regression created and tested.

Success metrics:
- Reduction in customer-reported ingestion errors for streaming structured outputs to <1% across canary tenants.
- False positive tool-call invocations due to misaligned events reduced by 95% in canary.
- No visible increase in P99 latency for streaming endpoints in canary (target +0ms to +5ms).

Technical approach (high level):
Phase 0 — Inventory and sample collection:
- Crawl existing incident logs, SDK error telemetry, and integration test failures to collect canonical failure examples.
- Create a small corpus of OpenAI Responses traces (stream transcripts, event-level JSON) representing real-world tool-calling + nested structured outputs.

Phase 1 — Detection & classification:
- Implement a sidecar analyzer that recognizes: incomplete JSON tokens across chunks, function-call markers (start/arg/complete), truncated finalization events, and inconsistent content-type frames.
- Classify deltas into categories (reassembly, ordering, truncated-metadata, tool-signal mismatch).

Phase 2 — Adapter design and proto:
- Design an adapter API that sits between runtime token consumer and public Responses translations. Key primitives: ReassemblyBuffer (bounded), EventFence markers, ToolCallAssembler, SchemaRepairPolicy (strict|lenient|auto).
- Runtime should allow config per-route: enable_adapter=true/false; policy profile; max-buffer-bytes.

Phase 3 — Implementation & profiling:
- Implement C++ hot-path pieces in serving runtime for reassembly, with fallbacks to fast JS/Go path in the translation layer when safe.
- Add continuous-batching-aware bookkeeping so adapter does not duplicate tokens across sharded requests.
- Instrument with metrics: adapter.reassemblies.count, adapter.latency.ms.histogram, adapter.schema_repairs.count, adapter.toolcall_normalizations.count.

Phase 4 — Harness, canary, and rollout:
- Build regression harness with recorded traces and unit tests asserting reconstructed objects and normalized tool calls.
- Canary: pick small set of internal customers + synthetic traffic; enable adapter in lenient mode by default.
- Monitor acceptance criteria and run 72h synthetic soak test.

Rollback triggers:
- Adapter increases P99 streaming latency >5ms above baseline for canary cluster for 30m window.
- Schema repair rate >0.5% of successful completions leading to semantically different outputs.
- New customer errors > baseline +3x for 1h.

Open questions and trade-offs:
1) Strict vs lenient defaults: Strict reduces downstream ambiguity but may reject borderline, causing higher user-visible failure; lenient may mask real semantic issues. Recommendation: default to lenient with logs + debug header for early adopters.
2) Buffer size vs latency: Reassembly requires buffering; must cap size to protect memory. Use adaptive shrink-on-idle heuristics.
3) Tool-call determinism: When we see multiple partial tool-call signals, should we coalesce heuristically or surface to SDKs? We'll prototype coalescing with a flag.

Artifacts and links: see references field for PRDs, prototype repos, and dashboards.
